title: Bhrigu Asks His Father
hookLine: a son asks his father to teach him Brahman, and the father only points: go find where everything comes from
carry: brahman: where everything comes from, lives in, returns to
tomorrow: salt disappears in a cup of water. where did it go?

cards: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, the god Varuna, and asks straight out: sir, teach me Brahman. And his father won't hand him an answer.

He gives him a few things to look at, food, breath, sight, hearing, mind, speech, and then one pointer. That from which these beings are born, by which they live, and into which they go when they leave: seek to know that.
That is Brahman. Then he sends his son off to find it himself.

teach.b: So Bhrigu sits with it, in tapas, deep, disciplined attention. He comes back: Brahman is food. Everything is born from food and lives on it.
His father doesn't argue. He just says: seek it again, through tapas. Keep looking.
Bhrigu goes deeper. Brahman is breath. Keep looking.
Brahman is mind. Keep looking. Brahman is understanding.
Keep looking. And the last time, Bhrigu understands: Brahman is bliss, ananda.
From bliss these beings are born, by bliss they live, into bliss they return. That's the big teaching.

teach.h: NOT A THING: THE SOURCE OF THINGS.
teach.b: Brahman isn't someone up in the sky, apart from the world, and it isn't one thing in the world. It's what the whole world comes from, rests in, and goes back to.
The Brahma Sutra's second line says almost exactly Varuna's words: Brahman is that from which the birth and so on of this world come.
Even schools that worship Brahman as a loving, personal God, like Ramanuja's, say the whole world lives within him.

teach.h: A BRANCH POINTING AT THE MOON.
teach.b: Vedanta teachers explain it with a picture: a parent shows a child the thin new moon by pointing at a branch just below it. The branch isn't the moon. It gets the eyes there.
The Upanishad gives another line too, Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite, and some readers, Shankara among them, hear even that as pointing. And notice how Bhrigu learned.
Each answer was true, and not the last word. Many teachers read his climb, food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss, as a path inward any seeker can walk.

how: In traditional Vedanta study, teachers explain the Brahma Sutra's second line alongside Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1 and 2.1, and the Bhriguvalli, Bhrigu's climb from food to bliss, is chanted and taught as part of the Taittiriya.

games.why: Varuna points Bhrigu to that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they go.

practice: Climb Bhrigu's steps slowly. Feel your body, fed by food. Then your breath, coming and going.
Then your mind, busy or quiet. Then the knowing that notices all of it. Then rest past the knowing, in whatever peace is there, without naming it.
If you pray, you can let that peace be your prayer to the One you love.

wordCard.voice: Vedanta. Today, how it points to Brahman: that from which the world is born, by which it lives, into which it returns, and, Bhrigu found, bliss. Today's word.
